Federico Balduini 1, Eunjung Cha1, Alberto Ferraris1, Nathan Drucker1, Heinz Schmid 1, Bernd Gotsmann 1& Cezar Zota 1

Cryogenic low-noise ampliﬁers employ high-electron mobility transistors to amplify the readout signals of quantum computers and quantum sensors. While these components beneﬁt from the cryogenic environment to achieve reduced noise levels, they are limited by self-heating, which causes a minimum noise level that is independent of the ambient temperature below 4-10 K. The characterization of self-heating has remained challenging, as traditional methods have relatively low temperature resolution and require elevated power levels to generate observable temperature increases. Furthermore, the phonon bath inside and around the device cannot readily be assumed to be in equilibrium with the electronic system. In this work, we use Shubnikov-de Haas quantum oscillation thermometry to determine the electron temperature in a high-performance cryogenic ampliﬁer with high temperature resolution. We detect four distinct regimes of energy dissipation, and ﬁnd links between self-heating, electron-electron interactions, i.e. hydrodynamic transport, as well as acoustic phonon emission. These insights can inform future ampliﬁer designs with improved resilience to self-heating and reduced noise, to support next-generation quantum computers.

In quantum computers, low-noise ampliﬁers (LNAs) are used to amplify extremely weak high-frequency electrical signals from qubit readout resonators1–3. The LNAs comprise passive matching networks and active transistors, commonly based on III-V compound semiconductor quantum wells such as the InAlAs/InGaAs/InP system4,5. The LNAs are commonly placed at the 4 K temperature stage of the cryostat, and located after a preampliﬁer stage based on superconducting parametric ampliﬁers2. The placement at the 4 K stage is essential to maintain a high signal-to-noise ratio due to the low power level of the signal, while placement at lower temperature stages is typically restricted by the relatively high power dissipation of the LNA2. It also enables LNAs to operate with lower noise and reduced power consumption, as several transistor characteristics improve at low temperature, notably the electron mobility and the subthreshold swing6–9. To support future quantum computers with increasing numbers of qubits, techniques to reduce the power dissipation and noise levels of LNA quantum well transistors are actively researched10. The minimum noise temperature (Tmin) refers to the lowest equivalent inputnoisetemperature(i.e.,theequivalentthermalnoiseofaresistoratthis temperature) which a transistor or LNA adds to the ampliﬁed input signal under optimal source impedance conditions, and is a key parameter for evaluating noise performance in transistors and LNAs10. Tg and Td are empirical parameters that represent the physical temperatures thatwouldproducethesameamountofthermalnoisepowerinthegateand the drain parts of the transistor. While Tg typically scales linearly with the ambient temperature, since the gate electrode is well thermalized with the environment, Td captures, among other things, hot electron effects and instead scales with the drain current, ID. In state-of-the-art LNAs, Tmin is about 2–4 K at 4–8 GHz with power consumption around 5–10 mW11–13. Due to the bias dependence of both fT and Td, Tmin is often approximated as the noise indication factor ﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃ ID p =gm, where ID is the drain current and gm (proportional to fT) is the transconductance. This highlights that, to achieve low Tmin, the transistor should show high transconductance gain at small operating current. At cryogenic conditions, this is typically achieved at gate biases close to the threshold voltage (usually ~0 V), and at relatively low drain biases, around 50–200 mV6. The Pospieszalski model proposes a link between the temperatures in the active area of the transistor, i.e., Tg and Td, and the noise of the LNA. Fundamentally, the thermal noise power increases with the charge carrier temperature, as Johnson-Nyquist noise is proportional to kBT. The increase of these temperatures above the ambient temperature conditions is caused by self-heating, i.e., dissipation of power due to resistive elements inside the transistors14. Inadditiontoimpactingnoiseperformance,self-heatingcanalsocause ampliﬁer back action, the effect of noise or thermal radiation propagating backwardfromtheampliﬁertothequantumprocessor18.Backaction,which has been linked to the temperature of the HEMT channel, can interact with qubits and degrade coherence19,20. In quantum computers, this effect is mitigated by placing circulators and isolators between the quantum processor and the ampliﬁer, which comes at the price of signal loss, cryostat space, and system complexity18. Various methods to characterize self-heating have previously been explored, including gate thermometry21, Schottky thermometry14,22, multispectral Raman thermometry23, infrared thermometry24, and pulsed/RF I-V measurements25. However, these techniques are limited when measuring self-heating at low power, i.e., low magnitudes of self-heating close to the Tmin of state-of-the-art LNAs. This is in part due to that these methods generally require a signiﬁcant temperature difference between the channel and the thermometer to obtain a clear signal, for instance when using an external part of the device as thermometer (such as the gate metal electrode)25,26. It is here important to distinguish the electron temperature, the effective temperature describing the energy distribution of the electrons, fromthecrystallatticetemperature,i.e.,thetemperatureofthephononbath. While these thermometry methods measure the lattice temperature only, high mobility semiconductors at cryogenic temperatures can exhibit a signiﬁcant difference between electron and lattice temperatures, as these two systems may fail to equilibrate effectively27,28. As an alternative, Shubnikov de Haas (SdH) thermometry instead measures the temperature of conduction band electrons through temperature-dependent quantum oscillations, and can be employed at ultra-low powers, potentially providing new insights into self-heating processes at temperature magnitudes close to technological relevant Tmin

29. In this paper, we use SdH thermometry to determine the mechanisms of self-heating in a high-performance cryogenic HEMT. We detect a sub- Kelvin rise of the electron temperature starting at 1.6 nW of applied DC power, along with a transition through four distinct self-heating regimes as electrons heat up due to increasing applied power. Notably, we identify a low-power regime dominated by electron-electron interactions that is followed by an onset of electron cooling through acoustic phonon emission near the Bloch-Grüneisen temperature.The expanded understanding of the self-heating processes at low power levels can guide efforts to realize lower electron temperatures at targeted operation points.

The role of electron-electron interactions In systems with multiple conducting subbands, i.e. the α and β subbands in this case, Landau level quantization gives rise to a resonance condition: Eβ  Eα ¼ kωc, where Ei is the energy at the bottom of a subband, k is an integer, and ωc is an effective cyclotron frequency based on the average cyclotron masses of the two subbands. When the magnetic ﬁeld causes Landau levels of each subband to become aligned, inter-subband scattering is strongly enhanced, thus the measured resistance increases. Between crossings, such scattering is suppressed, lowering the resistance. This process is called magneto inter-subband oscillation (MISO), and results in an oscillatory behavior periodic in 1/B38–40. Since MIS oscillations are driven by a scattering process, their amplitude is regulated by a scattering time τe, and shows an overall different temperature dependence than that of the SdH oscillations (described by the Lifshitz-Kosevich equation)39,41. Discussion We have shown that self-heating in cryogenic HEMTs, the rise of the electron temperature as a function of the applied bias, occurs through four scattering regimes (with T0 = 2 K as an example): (1) For low power, Te begins at T0, and electrons are heated by transfer of potential energy to kinetic energy (Joule heating) via movement through the source-drain electric ﬁeld in the transistor channel. While Te rises ~5 K in this regime, the lattice temperature is expected to be TL ≈T0, as electronphonon interactions are weak. (2) As the quantum well becomes fully populated by electrons, electron-electron (e-e) interactions increase, as shown by the valley in the differential resistance (the Gurzhi effect). Since e-e scattering is a momentum- and energy-conserving process within the electron system, it does not dissipate energy to the lattice. It is thus expected that the lattice temperature will remain TL ≈T0 also in this regime. When Te reaches around 25 K, e-e interactions are reduced due to the onset of phonon interactions, which can be deduced from the temperature-dependence of AMISO, and the powerdependence of the scattering time exponent, which transitions from ~2 to ~3 at the end of this region. (3) At this temperature, Joule heating slows down and the electron temperature is, within a range, nearly independent of the ambient temperature. As shown, this behavior is consistent with the emission of acoustic phonons as a cooling mechanism, via a deformation potential in the quantum well44,46. The efﬁciency of acoustic phonon emission depends on both the electron temperature and the conﬁnement of the quantum well, which altersphasespaceand the strength of electron-phononcoupling. Due to this process of thermal equilibration betweenthe electrons and the lattice, TL is expected to rise and approach the value of Te within this region. (4) As the lattice heats up from phonon emissions, electron transport becomes fully diffusive and dominated by electron-phonon scattering. Through this, the electric ﬁeld efﬁciently transfers energy to the lattice and both Te and TL rise rapidly, likely in equilibrium. 15.Inourmeasurements,asimilar effect is observed in the relative T0-independence of regions 3 and 4. No analytical model of Tmin as a function of either Te or TL exist, but it is generally known that the dominant noise mechanisms in a HEMT are shot noise and Johnson-Nyquist noise. For region 4, Te and TL are in thermodynamic equilibrium, but for regions 1–3, there is non-equilibrium as Te > TL. Under such conditions, the Johnson-Nyquist noise power will track the electron temperature, not the lattice temperature, as the ﬂuctuationdissipation relationship is governed by the actual thermal agitation of the charge carriers50. We thus expect that it is primarily Te that will cause excess noise in the LNA due to Johnson-Nyquist noise, i.e., that will limit Tmin. We note that there are also other sources of noise in a HEMT for which the link to Te is less clear, such as real-space transfer based on hot electrons, shot noise, and velocity ﬂuctuations51. In the Pospieszalski noise temperature model, the drain temperature, Td, describes the effective temperature of the drain-side electrons. Prior work has shown Td to be as high as 290 K at 7 µW/µm of power52. This compares with our value of Te ≈40 K at 5 µW/µm of power. With our

method, we measure the electron temperature through the temperaturedependence of the quantization of electron motion into Landau levels in a magnetic ﬁeld, which applies to electrons in the quantum well. On the other hand, Td refers to the temperature of electrons on the drain-side of the transistor, which is signiﬁcantly hotter than the channel due to Joule heating36. While operating the transistor at extremely low bias levels will result in lower Te (i.e., regions 1 and 2), overall, the noise performance, as well as the gain, will strongly degrade due to the reduced current. In addition, a minimum current is required to drive the passive circuitry of the LNA. Therefore, this is not a desirable approach. In general, region 3 appears to be the most attractive operation region, due to the relatively low and stable Te (compared to region 4), and the higher supported current. Conclusions We have here described the mechanisms of self-heating in a cryogenic ampliﬁer. Under low-ﬁeld conditions, hot electrons are generated by movement through the electric ﬁeld. As carriers heat up, electron-electron interactions become more numerous, resulting in hydrodynamic effects undercertainconditions.WhentheelectrontemperaturereachestheBloch- Grüneisen temperature, electrons are cooled down through acoustic phonon emission, which begins to heat up the crystal lattice. When the lattice and electron temperatures reach equilibrium, transport enters the diffusive regime, and self-heating rapidly increases. Based on this analysis, to further improve cryogenic LNAperformance for qubit readout, optimization of the phononicpropertiesofthequantumwellisapromisingpathforward,which includes aspects such as carrier density, chemical composition and conﬁnement.

Methods The probed HEMT device was fabricated following an industrial process ﬂow. It comprises a quantum well of 7 nm InAlAs/10 nm In0.70Ga0.30As/ 25 nm InAlAs on an InP substrate. The quantum well is delta-doped for a carrier concentration of 3e12 cm–2 at 4 K. A single device was isolated from

the chip and wire-bonded to the PPMS sample holder. While the HEMTs were designed in a typical ground-signal-ground high-frequency pad geometry with 2 gate ﬁngers, only one ﬁnger was probed at the time, thus only 3 out of the 4 available device pads were used. Typical cut-off and maximum oscillation frequencies for this chip were around 500 GHz each at 4 K. Subsequent measurements were performed using the PPMS to control temperature and magnetic ﬁeld, and two Zurich Instruments lock-in ampliﬁers for biasing and readout.
